title: us supreme court case tests fees immigration detainees 2026 08 13
text:
Aug 13 (Reuters) - (Billable Hours is Reuters' weekly report on lawyers and money. Please send tips or suggestions to D.Thomas@thomsonreuters.com
, opens new tab
.)
A construction worker from El Salvador is at the center of a U.S. Supreme Court fight over whether people who were wrongfully detained by immigration authorities can recoup attorney fees from the federal government
Lawyers for Kevin Montoya Palacios, 30, asked the justices to decide whether former detainees can recover legal fees under the 1980 Equal Access to Justice Act, which allows private parties who prevail in civil actions against the ​United States to recoup fees unless the government's position was "substantially justified" or "special circumstances make an award unjust."
The case hinges on whether immigration habeas corpus petition proceedings should be considered civil actions under the EAJA, a question that has divided ‌federal appeals courts. The 2nd, 3rd, 9th and 10th Circuit U.S. Courts of Appeal have concluded that habeas cases are civil actions. But the 4th Circuit disagreed in Montoya Palacios' case, as has the 5th Circuit.
The Supreme Court agreed in June to hear Montoya Palacios' case, and his brief is due August 31. If the high court sides with him, the federal government could be on the hook for attorney fees in other cases involving former immigration detainees.
Immigration attorneys told Reuters that the ability to recoup fees under the EAJA would encourage immigration attorneys to work on habeas petitions, as such cases can require hundreds of hours of legal work for ​clients who typically lack financial resources.
"It does cost us a lot of money," said Tedeisha Rowe, the founder and owner of immigration law firm American Legal Immigration Center in Silver Spring, Maryland. Rowe filed the habeas petition that led to Montoya Palacios' release.
​Republican President Donald Trump had launched aggressive immigration crackdown in his second term, sending out thousands of federal immigration agents to Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis and other Democratic-led cities. Judges have held more than ⁠4,400 times since October that Trump’s administration had detained immigrants unlawfully, a Reuters review of court records found.
William Evans, a Goodwin Procter partner representing Montoya Palacios pro bono in his Supreme Court appeal, said prior case law favors detainees on the issue of fees under the EAJA.
"There are ​literally centuries of United States law saying that immigration detention is civil in nature," he said.
The U.S. government, under both Republican and Democratic presidents, has argued that the statute's definition of civil action does not cover habeas petitions challenging immigration detention because those petitions are unique, functioning neither ​as civil nor criminal actions.
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to hear Montoya Palacios' case in a May filing, describing it as a "suitable vehicle for resolving the disagreement on an important and recurring legal question."
A spokesperson for the U.S. Justice Department declined to comment.
Montoya Palacios arrived in the United States in 2016. In 2023, he was granted immigration relief – called a withholding of removal – under the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, an international treaty that the U.S. ratified in 1988. He was able to corroborate that he was being persecuted by the Mara Salvatrucha gang, or MS-13, due to his job ​as a utilities provider, Rowe said.
He was detained by ICE during a routine check-in with the Department of Homeland Security in December, Rowe said.
ICE moved Montoya Palacios to government facilities in different states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, Kentucky and Louisiana, and he was almost sent back to El Salvador ​before he was released in early February after a federal judge ruled his detention was unlawful, his attorneys said. He has been reunited with his wife and two children, Rowe said.
A Baltimore federal judge in February denied Montoya Palacios' bid to recoup nearly $9,000 in attorney fees and costs. The 4th Circuit ‌upheld the decision ⁠in March.
In a related case now before the Supreme Court, two detainees were awarded more than $33,000 in fees under the EAJA after they were found to have been wrongfully detained in the Philipsburg, Pennsylvania, ICE facility. The 3rd Circuit in February upheld the fee awards.
The U.S. government filed its own Supreme Court petition in July to review the cases. The court has not yet ruled whether it will grant the petition.
Evans said the amount of potential attorney fees at stake in immigration proceedings was unclear.
"Not immaterial, not nothing, but also not something that's going to stop the government in its tracks from pursuing its enforcement priorities," he said.
A win for immigration detainees at the Supreme Court would not automatically entitle successful habeas petitioners to recoup fees, said Jesse Lempel, a Goodwin Procter associate who is also representing Montoya Palacios. Fees are awarded on a case-by-case basis, and the ​government could still argue that its detention of a particular person was ​substantially justified.
"You don’t automatically get fees because you win," Lempel ⁠said.
Fees under the EAJA are most commonly awarded in cases involving disputed Social Security and veterans' benefits. Federal agencies paid more than $128 million in legal fee awards and expenses under the law between October 1, 2024 and September 30, 2025, according to a March 26 report from the Administrative Conference of the United States.
Law firm MSO deals face headwinds in Chicago, fresh interest in New York
Illinois' governor on Friday signed a bill into law ​prohibiting any entity involved in a law firm's legal practice but not fully owned by lawyers from interfering with attorneys' professional judgment, controlling hiring decisions or revealing client documents.
The Illinois law is largely ​aimed at law firm management services organizations (MSOs), ⁠which allow law firms to receive outside capital by spinning off their non-legal, back-office operations like human resources or marketing into a separate organization owned or partly owned by outside investors.
The law does not bar law firm MSOs but could limit how they operate in the state.
In New York, meanwhile, 150-lawyer Ellenoff Grossman & Schole has been engaged in “lengthy deliberations” about potentially launching an MSO, including conversations with ethics lawyers, investors, auditors and other law firms, its founder Douglas Ellenoff told Reuters.
Ellenoff said his firm, which is known for its work on deals involving special purpose acquisition companies (SPAC), was first approached about a decade ago ⁠about a possible ​investment but “we couldn’t get comfortable” at the time, he said.
Now, he said, “I think that this has a lot more momentum to it than previous iterations." He said the ​firm has not made a decision yet on whether to proceed with an MSO.

--The Kennedy Center was ordered to pay more than $250,000 in legal fees to a jazz musician who defeated the center's lawsuit over ​his refusal to perform at a Christmas Eve event after President Donald Trump renamed the building after himself.
